content:
The European Commission has paid Ukraine €7.9 billion in a single transfer, the largest one-off payment Brussels has made to Kyiv since Russia's full-scale invasion began, the Commission announced on Friday.

The disbursement, worth €7,859,441,144 in exact terms, was released on 20 November under the Ukraine Facility, the European Union's main instrument for supporting Ukraine's recovery, reform programme and path towards EU membership. It is the ninth tranche under the facility and the biggest single payment in its history, according to the [European Commission](https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-disburses-eur79-billion-strengthen-ukraines-financial-stability-and-advance-reform-2026-11-20_en).

"Ukraine continues to deliver on reforms, while defending itself each and every day," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement. "Today, we are disbursing nearly €8 billion — this is the largest payment made so far."

The money is intended to cover Ukraine's financing needs and keep the country's public administration running as the war grinds on. Kyiv confirmed the funds had reached the state budget. Prime Minister Sergi Koretski thanked von der Leyen, the Commission and all EU member states "for your trust, your constant support and your concrete decisions that strengthen Ukraine", in a message on social media after the transfer.

The payment was unlocked after Ukraine completed more than 20 agreed reform steps, spanning the judiciary, the fight against corruption and money laundering, energy, agriculture and the environment. The EU Council signed off on the tranche on 16 November, and the Commission paid it four days later. Cash-for-reforms is the core logic of the Ukraine Facility: money flows in tranches only as Kyiv meets the milestones in its Ukraine Plan, the roadmap tied to its EU membership bid.

Of the €7.9 billion, €5.1 billion comes from the Ukraine Support Loan, the €90 billion facility agreed in April 2026 to cover Ukraine's needs over 2026 and 2027. With this payment, more than €5.9 billion has now been disbursed through the loan component of the facility. The loan itself is split €60 billion for defence capabilities and the defence industry and €30 billion for budgetary needs and the functioning of the state.

The disbursement also unlocked fresh public investment. According to the Commission, Ukraine has mobilised €948 million in public investment alongside the payment, directed at education, healthcare, housing and the demining of agricultural land — work that matters as much to the country's long-term recovery as the budget support itself.

The scale of the payment reflects how tight Ukraine's finances have become. Brussels estimates Kyiv faces a financing gap of roughly €70 billion in 2027 alone. On 18 November, just two days before the money landed, the Commission proposed up to €45 billion in additional financial support for Ukraine in 2027, a proposal that still needs approval from member states. For the rest of 2026, a further €15.7 billion in EU financial support remains available to Ukraine, of which more than €14 billion would come through the Ukraine Support Loan — including €10.2 billion to strengthen defence and industrial capabilities and €3.9 billion in budget support. Any further release, however, is conditional on Kyiv completing the agreed reforms.

The Ukraine Facility entered into force on 1 March 2024 and provides more than €50 billion in grants and loans to support Ukraine over 2024–2027, excluding external contributions from member states and partner countries and funds from the Ukraine Support Loan. With Friday's payment, total EU support under the facility since mid-2024 will reach €40 billion, according to European Pravda.

The broader picture is larger still. Following this disbursement, the EU and its member states have provided €245.5 billion in overall support to Ukraine since 2022, the Commission said — including €3.8 billion drawn from the proceeds of immobilised Russian assets, a funding source that has become increasingly central to the debate over how to sustain Kyiv.

The payment lands in a week when the war's costs have been brutally visible. On Friday night a Russian ballistic missile struck Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's home town, killing a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman and wounding 60 people, according to local officials. The strike underlined why the budget support matters: behind the front line, Ukraine must keep paying soldiers, teachers, doctors and pensioners while its cities are under attack.

It also comes as the EU tries to lock in longer-term financing. The €45 billion proposal for 2027, unveiled on 18 November, is designed to close part of next year's gap, but it arrives alongside a separate debate over the bloc's next seven-year budget, in which European Council President António Costa has proposed a 3% levy on large technology companies' digital revenues to help pay for EU spending — a reminder that Ukraine's funding competes with other priorities in Brussels. Readers can follow that budget debate in our coverage of [Costa's digital tax proposal](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/costa-eu-digital-tax-3-percent-november-2026).

The Commission said it remains fully committed to delivering the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027, as well as the remaining funds under the initial Ukraine Facility. For Kyiv, the message is that the money will keep flowing — but only as long as the reforms do. The next test will come before the year ends, when further tranches depend on Ukraine completing the remaining conditions attached to the €15.7 billion still available in 2026. Military support continues in parallel: NATO allies have also committed $10 billion in US weapons purchases for Ukraine, as reported in our coverage of the [NATO allies' weapons package](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/nato-allies-10-billion-us-weapons-ukraine-november-2026).

Whether the EU can sustain this pace into 2027 will depend on two things: member states approving the additional €45 billion, and Ukraine continuing to deliver the reforms that unlock each payment. Friday's record transfer shows both sides, for now, are holding up their end of the bargain.
summary: The European Commission released €7.9 billion to Ukraine on 20 November — the largest single payment under the Ukraine Facility — after Kyiv completed more than 20 reform steps, with €5.1 billion drawn from the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan.
title: EU disburses record €7.9 billion to Ukraine in largest single payment of the war
